title: Of the art of conference
paragraphs: Our justice has a custom of condemning some as a warning to others. To condemn them simply for having done wrong would be folly, as Plato says,
[Diogenes Laertius, however, in his Life of Plato, iii. 181, says that Plato's offence was speaking too freely to the tyrant.]

for what is done can never be undone; rather it's to keep them from offending again, and so others may avoid the example of their offence. We do not correct the man we hang; we correct others through him. I do the same. My errors are sometimes natural, incorrigible, and beyond remedy; but the good which virtuous men do for the public by making themselves models to imitate, I may perhaps do by making my own manners something to be avoided:
"Nonne vides, Albi ut male vivat filius? utque Barrus inops? magnum documentum, ne patriam rem perdere quis velit;"
["Do you not see how badly the son of Albus lives? And the poor Barrus? A great warning, lest anyone be inclined to squander his inheritance." — Horace, Sat., i. 4, 109.]

by publishing and exposing my own faults, someone may learn to fear them. The parts of myself I value most gain more honour from being criticised than from being praised — which is why I so often fall into that mode and dwell on it. But all things considered, a man never speaks of himself without losing something. A man's accusations against himself are always believed; his praises never. There may, perhaps, be some of my own temperament who learn better through contrast than through likeness, by avoiding rather than by imitating. The elder Cato was thinking of this kind of discipline when he said "the wise may learn more from fools than fools can from the wise"; and Pausanias tells us of an ancient harp player who used to send his pupils to listen to a very bad musician who lived across the street, so they would learn to hate his discords and false rhythms. The horror of cruelty inclines me to clemency more than any example of clemency could. A good rider does not improve my seat as much as an awkward lawyer or a Venetian on horseback does; and a clownish way of speaking reforms mine more than the most polished does. The ridiculous and foolish look of another always warns and instructs me. What pricks and rouses incites much better than what tickles. The time is now ripe for us to reform backwards — more by dissent than by agreement, more by difference than by consent. Profiting little from good examples, I make use of the bad ones, which are everywhere to be found. I try to make myself as agreeable as I see others offensive, as constant as I see others fickle, as gentle as I see others harsh, as good as I see others evil. But I set myself impossible standards.

The most fruitful and natural exercise of the mind, in my view, is conversation. I find its use sweeter than any other action in life — which is why, if I were now forced to choose, I think I would sooner consent to lose my sight than my hearing and speech. The Athenians, and also the Romans, kept this exercise in great honour in their academies. The Italians retain some traces of it to this day, much to their advantage, as is clear when you compare their understandings with ours. The study of books is a languid and feeble motion that does not heat the blood, whereas conversation teaches and exercises at once. If I converse with a strong mind and a rough disputant, he presses upon my flanks and pricks me from right and left; his thoughts stir up mine; jealousy, glory, and contention drive and raise me to something above myself; and easy agreement is a tedious quality in any discussion. But while our mind fortifies itself by contact with vigorous and well-ordered minds, it is impossible to say how much it loses and degrades by the constant company and familiarity of mean and feeble spirits. No contagion spreads like that one; I know well enough from experience what a yard of it costs. I love to discuss and dispute, but only with a few men, and for my own sake; doing it as a spectacle and entertainment for great persons, making a competitive parade of one's wit and words, is in my opinion very unbecoming a man of honour.

Folly is a bad quality; but to be unable to bear it, to fret and chafe at it as I do, is another kind of disease, scarcely less troublesome than folly itself — and it is the thing I am now going to accuse in myself. I enter into conference and dispute with great freedom and ease, since opinion finds in me a soil very unsuited to penetration, where it can take no deep root. No proposition astonishes me, no belief offends me, however contrary to my own; there is no notion so frivolous and extravagant that it doesn't seem to me a possible product of the human mind. We who deprive our judgment of the right to decide look indifferently on differing opinions, and even if we don't lean our judgment toward them, we easily give them a hearing. Where one side of the scale is completely empty, I let the other waver under an old wife's dreams; and I think myself excused if I prefer the odd number; Thursday rather than Friday; if I would rather be the twelfth or fourteenth at table than the thirteenth; if I would rather, on a journey, see a hare run past me than cross my path; if I would rather give my servant my left foot than my right when he comes to put on my stockings. All such fancies that have any currency around us deserve at least a hearing. For my part they only register with me as empty, but they do register. Moreover, common and casual opinions are something more than nothing in nature, and the man who will not let himself go that far may fall into the vice of obstinacy to avoid the vice of superstition.

The contradictions of judgments, then, neither offend nor alter me; they only rouse and exercise me. We dodge correction, when we ought to offer and present ourselves to it, especially when it comes in the form of conversation rather than authority. At every opposition, we do not consider whether or not it has merit; right or wrong, we look only for how to extricate ourselves. Instead of opening our arms, we put out our claws. I could bear to be roughly handled by my friend, even to be told I'm a fool and don't know what I'm talking about. I love strong expression among gentlemen, and to have them say what they really think; we must fortify and harden our hearing against this tenderness for the ceremonious sound of words. I love a strong and manly familiarity and conversation — a friendship that pleases itself in the sharpness and vigour of its exchange, like love in biting and scratching. It is not vigorous and generous enough if it is not quarrelsome; if it is too civilised and artificial, if it treads carefully and shies at every shock:
"Neque enim disputari sine reprehensione potest."
["Nor can people dispute without reprehension." — Cicero, De Finib., i. 8.]

When someone contradicts me, he raises my attention, not my anger. I move toward the man who challenges me, who instructs me; the cause of truth ought to be the common cause of both of us. What will the angry man answer? Passion has already confounded his judgment; agitation has taken the place of reason. It would not be a bad thing if the outcome of our disputes were settled by wager, so that there might be some material mark of our losses, the better to remember them; so that my servant could tell me, "Your ignorance and obstinacy cost you a hundred crowns last year, on this and that occasion." I welcome and embrace truth wherever I find it, and surrender to it cheerfully, opening my conquered arms as soon as I see it coming. And, provided it isn't done too imperiously, I take pleasure in being corrected, and accommodate myself to my accusers — very often more out of civility than out of any sense that I need amending — gladly nourishing the freedom to admonish me by how easily I submit to it, even at my own expense.

Still, it is hard to bring the men of my time to this: they have not the courage to correct, because they have not the courage to be corrected, and they always speak with dissimulation in each other's presence. I take such pleasure in being judged and known that it is almost a matter of indifference to me which of the two forms it takes. My imagination contradicts and condemns itself so often that I don't mind if someone else does the same, especially since I give his reproof no greater authority than I choose. But I break with the man who carries himself too high — I know one who repents of his advice if it isn't believed, and takes it as an affront if it isn't immediately followed. That Socrates always received with a smile the contradictions offered to his arguments could be put down to the strength of his reason: since the advantage was bound to fall on his side, he welcomed them as the material of a new victory. But we see, on the contrary, that nothing in argument makes our feelings as touchy as the conviction of our own pre-eminence and our disdain for the adversary; and yet in reason it's the weaker who should take in good part the corrections that set him right. In earnest, I prefer the company of those who ruffle me to those who fear me; it is a dull and harmful pleasure to deal with people who admire us and approve of everything we say. Antisthenes told his children never to take it kindly or as a favour when anyone praised them. I find I am much prouder of the victory I win over myself, when in the very heat of dispute I make myself submit to my opponent's force of reason, than I am pleased with any victory I win over him through his weakness. In short, I accept and admit any sort of attack that is direct, no matter how weak; but I have no patience with those that come at me out of form. I don't care what the subject is, the opinions are all the same to me, and I am almost indifferent whether I come off best or worst. I can argue peaceably for a whole day if the argument is conducted with method; I don't ask so much for force and subtlety as for order — I mean the kind of order we daily see among the wranglings of shepherds and shop boys, but never among us: if they stray from their subject, it is out of incivility, and so it is with us; but their tumult and impatience never knock them off topic; their argument keeps its course. If they interrupt and don't wait for one another, at least they understand one another. Anyone answers me well enough if he answers what I actually said. When the dispute is irregular and disordered, I leave the matter itself and insist on the form, with anger and indiscretion, falling into a willful, malicious, and imperious style of disputation, which I am afterwards ashamed of. It's impossible to deal fairly with a fool: my judgment is not only corrupted under the hand of so impetuous a master, but my conscience is too.

Our disputes ought to be forbidden and punished like other verbal crimes. What vice do they not stir up and pile on top of each other, being always driven and commanded by passion? We first quarrel with the reasons, and then with the men. We only learn to dispute so that we may contradict; and so, with everyone contradicting and being contradicted, the fruit of disputation turns out to be the loss and annihilation of truth. That is why Plato in his Republic forbids this exercise to fools and the ill-bred. What's the point of trying to inquire into anything with someone who knows nothing relevant? A man does no harm to the subject when he leaves it to consider how it should be handled — I don't mean in some artificial, scholastic way, but in a natural way, with good sense. What will it come to in the end? One man flies east, another west; they lose the main point, scattering it in the crowd of side issues. After an hour of storm, they no longer know what they're looking for: one is below the subject, another above, a third off to the side. One catches at a word and a simile; another no longer hears what is being said against him, thinking only of pursuing his own track, not of answering you; another, finding himself too weak to make a stand, fears everything, refuses everything, confuses the subject from the start, or, at the height of the dispute, stops short and falls silent, his peevish ignorance pretending either a proud contempt or a foolishly modest avoidance of further debate. Provided this man can land a blow, he doesn't care how much he leaves himself open. Another counts his words and weighs them as if they were arguments. Another only brawls, relying on his lungs. Here's one who learnedly concludes against himself, and another who deafens you with prefaces and senseless digressions. Another falls into downright abuse and picks a quarrel in the German fashion, to extricate himself from a wit pressing too hard on him. And a last man sees nothing into the reason of the thing but draws a line of siege-works around you out of dialectical clauses and the formulas of his art.
Now, who would not begin to mistrust the sciences and doubt whether he can reap any solid fruit from them for the service of life, given the use we make of them?
"Nihil sanantibus litteris."
["Letters which cure nothing." — Seneca, Ep., 59.]
Who has gained understanding through his logic? Where are all logic's fine promises?
"Nec ad melius vivendum, nec ad commodius disserendum."
["It makes a man neither live better nor talk better." — Cicero, De Fin., i. 19.]

Is there more noise or confusion in the scolding of fishwives than in the public disputes of men of this profession? I would rather my son learn to speak in a tavern than to babble in the schools. Take a master of arts and have a conversation with him; why doesn't he make us feel that artificial excellence? Why doesn't he captivate women and ignoramuses like us with admiration at the steadiness of his reasons and the beauty of his order? Why doesn't he sway and persuade us to whatever he wants? Why does a man, with so much advantage in matter and treatment, mix abuse, indiscretion, and fury into his arguments? Strip him of his gown, his hood, and his Latin; let him not batter our ears with pure unadulterated Aristotle, and you'll take him for one of us, or worse. While they torment us with this complication and confusion of words, it goes with them, it seems to me, as with conjurors: their dexterity imposes on our senses but does not work on our belief at all. Apart from this sleight of hand, they perform nothing that is not very ordinary and mean: for being more learned, they are no less foolish.
[So Hobbes said that if he had read as much as the academic pedants he should have known as little.]

I love and honour knowledge as much as those who have it, and in its true use it is the most noble and the greatest of human acquisitions; but in such people as I'm speaking of (and there are countless of them), who build their fundamental sufficiency and value upon it, who appeal from their understanding to their memory:
"Sub aliena umbra latentes,"
["Sheltering under the shadow of others." — Seneca, Ep., 33.]

and who can do nothing except out of a book — I hate it, if I dare say so, worse than stupidity. In my country, and in my time, learning improves fortunes well enough, but not minds. If it meets with minds that are dull and heavy, it overburdens and suffocates them, leaving them a crude undigested mass; if it meets with airy, fine minds, it purifies, clarifies, and refines them to the point of evaporation. It is almost a neutral thing: a very useful accessory to a well-born soul, but harmful and pernicious to others — or rather a thing of very precious use, that won't let itself be bought at a discount. In the hand of some, it is a sceptre; in the hand of others, a fool's bauble.

But let us continue. What greater victory do you expect than to make your enemy see and know that he can't stand up to you? When you get the better of your argument, it is the truth that wins; when you get the better of the form and method, it is you who win. I think that in Plato and Xenophon, Socrates disputes more for the sake of the disputants than for the sake of the dispute, and more to instruct Euthydemus and Protagoras in the knowledge of their own impertinence than in the impertinence of their art. He takes hold of the first subject like a man with a more profitable end in view than to explain it — namely, to clear the understandings of those he sets out to instruct and exercise. Hunting after truth is properly our business, and we are inexcusable if we carry on the chase ineptly and badly; failing to seize it is another matter, for we are born to inquire after truth: it belongs to a greater power to possess it. As Democritus said, truth is not hidden at the bottom of the deeps, but rather lifted to an infinite height in the divine knowledge. The world is only a school of inquiry: it is not a question of who shall enter the ring, but of who shall run the best course. A man who speaks the truth can play the fool just as easily as one who speaks falsehoods, for we are concerned with the manner of speaking, not the matter. It is my temper to attend to the form as much as to the substance, and to the advocate as much as to the cause, as Alcibiades told us we should. Every day I spend my time reading authors without any consideration of what they're learned in; their manner is what I look for, not their subject. And just so do I pursue the conversation of any distinguished wit — not so that he may teach me, but so that I may know him, and so that, knowing him, if I think him worth imitating, I may imitate him. Every man may speak truly, but to speak with method, prudence, and fullness is a talent few men have. The falsity that comes from ignorance does not offend me, but the foppery of it does. I have broken off several negotiations that would have been to my advantage because of the impertinent wrangling of those I was dealing with. I am not moved once a year by the faults of those under my authority, but on account of the ridiculous obstinacy of their claims, denials, and excuses we are at each other's throats every day. They neither understand what is said, nor why, and they answer accordingly; it's enough to drive a man mad. I never feel any blow to my head except when it is knocked against another, and I more easily forgive the vices of my servants than their boldness, their pestering, and their folly. Let them do less, provided they understand what they're doing. You live in hope of warming their affection for your service, but there is nothing to be had, nothing to be expected, from a block of wood.

But what if I take things otherwise than they are? Perhaps I do, and that is why I accuse my own impatience, holding in the first place that it is equally a vice in the man who is in the right and in the man who is in the wrong — for it is always a tyrannical sourness not to endure a form contrary to one's own. And besides, there is in truth no greater, more constant, more disorderly folly than to be moved and angered by the follies of the world, for it makes us quarrel chiefly with ourselves. The old philosopher never wanted for an occasion of tears while he considered himself. Miso, one of the seven sages, of a Timonian and Democritic temper, when asked what he was laughing at, alone, answered: "At the fact that I am laughing alone." How many ridiculous things, by my own judgment, do I say and answer every day of my life? And then how many more, by the judgment of others? If I bite my own lips, what should others do? In the end, we must live among the living and let the river run on under the bridge without our worrying about it — or, at any rate, without our interfering. Truly, why do we encounter a man with a hunchback or some other deformity without being moved, and yet cannot tolerate meeting a deformed mind without flying into a temper? This vicious sourness belongs more to the judge than to the crime. Let us always have this saying of Plato on our lips: "Don't I think things unsound because I am not sound myself? Am I not myself at fault? Might not my own observations reflect on me?" — a wise and divine saying that lashes the most universal and common error of mankind. Not only the reproaches we throw in one another's faces, but our reasons too, our arguments, and our controversies, can rebound on us, and we wound ourselves with our own weapons; antiquity has left me plenty of grave examples of this. It was ingeniously and tellingly said by the man who invented this sentence:
"Stercus cuique suum bene olet."
["To every man his own excrement smells fine." — Erasmus]

We see nothing behind us; we mock ourselves a hundred times a day when we mock our neighbours; and we hate in others the very defects which are more obvious in ourselves, and which we admire with marvellous obliviousness and brazenness. Only yesterday I heard a man of understanding and good rank scoffing as pleasantly as he was justified at the folly of another man who did nothing but torment everyone with the catalogue of his genealogy and alliances — more than half of them false (for those whose status is most doubtful and least secure are the most apt to fall into such ridiculous talk) — and yet, had he looked into himself, he would have found himself just as intemperate and tedious in extolling his wife's pedigree. O importunate presumption, with which the wife sees herself armed by the very hands of her own husband. If he understood Latin, we should say to him:
"Age, si hic non insanit satis sua sponte, instiga."
["Come! If of himself he is not mad enough, urge him on." — Terence, And., iv. 2, 9.]

I am not saying that no man should accuse another unless he himself is clean — for then no one would ever accuse — clean of the same kind of stain; rather I mean that our judgment, falling upon another who is currently in question, ought not at the same time to spare ourselves, but should sentence us with an inward and severe authority. It is an act of charity that a man who cannot cure himself of a vice should nevertheless try to remove it from another, in whom it may perhaps not have so deep and so malignant a root. Nor do I tell the man who reproves me for a fault that he himself is guilty of the same. What of it? The reproof is true all the same, and of very good use. If we had a good nose, our own ordure would stink worse to us, just because it is our own. And Socrates is of the opinion that whoever should find himself, his son, and a stranger guilty of some violence and wrong ought to begin with himself, present himself first to the sentence of justice, and to purge himself, beg the assistance of the executioner's hand; then proceed to his son, and lastly to the stranger. If this precept seems too severe, at least the man ought to present himself first to the punishment of his own conscience.

The senses are our first and proper judges, and they perceive things only through external accidents; no wonder, then, that throughout the service of our society there is so constant and universal a mixture of ceremonies and surface appearances — to the point that the best and most effective part of our politics consists in just these. We are still dealing with man, whose condition is wonderfully bodily. Let those who, in recent years, have wanted to set up for us such a contemplative and immaterial exercise of religion not be surprised if there are some who think it would have vanished and melted through their fingers had it not held itself up among us more as a banner, title, and instrument of division and faction than by itself. As in conference, the gravity, robe, and fortune of the speaker often give weight to vain arguments and idle words, it is hard not to assume that a man so attended and feared has more than ordinary capacity, and that one to whom the king has given so many offices, commissions, and charges, so proud and supercilious, has a great deal more in him than another who greets him from a respectful distance and holds no office at all. Not only the words but the very grimaces of these people are considered and weighed, with everyone making it his business to give them some fine, solid interpretation. If they stoop to common conversation, and you offer anything but approval and reverence, they knock you down with the authority of their experience: they have heard, they have seen, they have done such-and-such; you are crushed under examples. I would gladly tell them that the fruit of a surgeon's experience is not the history of his practice and his remembering that he has cured four people of the plague and three of the gout, unless he knows how to extract from this something on which to form his judgment, and to make us feel that he has thereby become more skilled in his art. As in a concert of instruments, we don't hear a lute, a harpsichord, or a flute by itself, but one entire harmony, the result of all together. If travel and offices have improved them, it's the product of their understanding to make it show. It's not enough to count up experiences — they must be weighed, sorted, and distilled to extract the reasons and conclusions they carry within them. There were never so many historians; it is indeed good, and useful, to read them, for they everywhere furnish us with excellent and praiseworthy lessons from the magazine of their memory, which is doubtless of great help in living. But that's not what we are looking for now: we are asking whether these relaters and collectors of things are themselves worth anything.

I hate all sorts of tyranny, in word and in deed. I am very ready to set myself against those vain trappings that deceive our judgment through the senses; and keeping a close eye on those extraordinary greatnesses, I find that at best they are men just like the rest:
"Rarus enim ferme sensus communis in illa Fortuna."
["For in those high fortunes, common sense is generally rare." — Juvenal, viii. 73.]

Perhaps we esteem and look up to them at less than they really are, because they undertake more and expose themselves more; they don't measure up to the burden they have taken on. There has to be more vigour and strength in the carrier than in the load. A man who has not lifted as much as he can leaves you to guess that he still has strength in reserve, that he has not been tested to the limit of what he can do; a man who collapses under his load lays his best on display, along with the weakness of his shoulders. This is why we see so many silly souls among the learned — more of them than among those of better stock. They would have made good farmers, good merchants, and good artisans; their natural vigour was cut to that proportion. Knowledge is a thing of great weight, and they sink under it. Their understanding has neither the vigour nor the dexterity to display and distribute, to put to use, this rich and powerful matter. It has prevailing power only in a strong nature, and such natures are very rare — and the weak ones, says Socrates, corrupt the dignity of philosophy in the handling. It seems useless and vicious when lodged in an ill-formed mind. They spoil themselves and make fools of themselves:
"Humani qualis simulator simius oris, Quem puer arridens pretioso stamine serum Velavit, nudasque nates ac terga reliquit, Ludibrium mensis."

["Just like an ape, that mimic of the human face, whom a teasing boy has dressed up in rich silks above but left the lower parts bare, for a laughing-stock at the tables." — Claudian, in Eutrop., i. 303.]

Nor is it enough for those who govern and command us, and who hold the whole world in their hands, to have a common understanding, to be able to do what we can do; they fall far below us if they are not infinitely above us. As they promise more, so they have to deliver more.

And yet for them silence is not only a face of respect and gravity, but very often of great advantage too. For when Megabyzus went to see Apelles in his painting room, he stood a long while without speaking a word, and finally began to talk about the paintings — for which he was given this blunt rebuke: "While you were silent you seemed something great, because of your chains and rich dress; but now that we have heard you speak, there is not the meanest boy in my workshop who does not despise you." Those princely ornaments, that mighty state, did not permit him to be ignorant with a common ignorance, or to speak impertinently of painting; he ought to have kept that external, presumptive knowledge intact by remaining silent. To how many of the foolish fellows of my time has a sullen, silent demeanour brought the credit of prudence and capacity!

Dignities and offices are necessarily given out more by fortune than on account of merit, and we are often wrong to blame the kings when these are misplaced; on the contrary, it is a wonder that they have such good luck where there is so little skill involved:
"Principis est virtus maxima nosse suos;"
["It is the chief virtue of a prince to know his own people." — Martial, viii. 15.]

for nature has not given them a sight that can extend to so many people, to discern which of them excels the rest, nor to see into our hearts where the knowledge of our wills and our real worth lies. They have to choose us by conjecture and groping — by family, wealth, learning, and popular reputation, all of them very feeble grounds. Whoever could find a way for kings to judge by justice and to choose men by reason would by that single thing establish a perfect form of government.

"Ah, but he brought that great affair to a successful conclusion." That is to say something, but not enough; for the saying is justly received that "we are not to judge of counsels by their outcomes." The Carthaginians punished the bad counsel of their captains even when it was salvaged by a successful issue; and the Roman people often refused a triumph for great and very advantageous victories because the general's conduct didn't match his good fortune. We commonly see, in the actions of the world, that Fortune, to show us her power in all things, and taking pride in deflating our presumption, since she could not make fools wise, has made them fortunate in rivalry with virtue. She favours most those operations the web of which is most purely her own — which is why the simplest among us bring great affairs to pass, both public and private. As Seiramnes the Persian answered those who wondered that his affairs turned out so badly when his deliberations were so wise: "I am sole master of my designs, but success is wholly in the power of fortune." These men might answer the same, only with the opposite spin. Most worldly affairs perform themselves:
"Fata viam inveniunt;"
["The destinies find the way." — Aeneid, iii. 395.]

the outcome often justifies a very foolish course of action; our interference is little more than running on by rote, and more usually a matter of custom and example than of reason. Having been amazed at the greatness of some affair, I have been told by those who carried it out how it was done, and have found nothing but very ordinary calculations. The most common and ordinary ones are perhaps the surest and most convenient in practice, if not in display. What if the plainest reasons are the best founded? The meanest, lowest, and most beaten the best suited to affairs? To maintain the authority of the counsels of kings, it is not needed that profane persons should take part in them, or see further into them than the outer barrier; he who would husband its reputation must be reverenced on credit and taken altogether. My consultation roughs out the matter a little and considers it lightly by the first face it shows; the weight and main of the business I have made a habit of leaving to heaven:
"Permitte divis caetera."
["Leave the rest to the gods." — Horace, Od., i. 9, 9.]

Good and ill fortune are, in my opinion, two sovereign powers; it is folly to think that human prudence can play the part of Fortune; and vain is the man who imagines he can grasp both causes and consequences and conduct the progress of his design by the hand — most especially vain in the deliberations of war. There was never greater circumspection and military prudence than is sometimes seen among us; can it be that men are afraid of losing themselves on the way, that they save themselves up for the end of the game? Moreover, I affirm that our wisdom and counsel for the most part submit themselves to the conduct of chance. My will and my reason are sometimes moved by one breath and sometimes by another, and many of these movements are governed without me; my reason has uncertain and accidental impulses:
"Vertuntur species animorum, et pectora motus Nunc alios, alios, dum nubila ventus agebat, Concipiunt."
["The aspects of their minds change; and they conceive now one set of ideas, now another, just so long as the wind keeps stirring the clouds." — Virgil, Georg., i. 42.]

Just observe who carry the greatest authority in cities, and who best run their own affairs; you will find they are usually men of the lowest abilities. Women, children, and madmen have had the fortune to govern great kingdoms as well as the wisest princes, and Thucydides says that the stupid more often do it than men of better understanding. We attribute the effects of their good fortune to their prudence:
"Ut quisque Fortuna utitur, Ita praecellet; atque exinde sapere illum omnes dicimus;"
["He makes his way who knows how to use Fortune, and on that account we all call him wise." — Plautus, Pseudol., ii. 3, 13.]
and so I say without reservation: outcomes are a very poor testimony of our worth and parts.

Now, I was making this point — that you need only see a man promoted to high office; though three days before we held him in little regard, an image of grandeur and capacity insensibly creeps into our view, and we persuade ourselves that, since he is increased in reputation and retinue, he must be increased in merit too. We judge him not by his worth but, like counters, by the value of the place he occupies. If he happens to fall again and be mixed back into the common crowd, everyone asks in amazement how he ever came to be raised so high. "Is this him?" they say. "Did he know no more when he was up there? Do princes content themselves with so little? We were truly in good hands." This is something I have often seen in my time. Even the mere disguise of grandeur put on stage in our comedies in some sense moves and gulls us. What I myself adore in kings is the crowd of their adorers. All reverence and submission are due to them, except that of the understanding. My reason is not obliged to bow and bend; my knees are. Melanthius, asked what he thought of the tragedy of Dionysius, said, "I couldn't see it — it was so clouded over with language"; so most of those who judge the speeches of great men ought to say, "I didn't understand the words, they were so clouded with gravity, grandeur, and majesty." Antisthenes one day tried to persuade the Athenians to order their donkeys to be used in tilling the ground, just as horses were; he was told that that animal was not destined for such service. "That's all the same to me," he replied; "you have only to order it. For the most ignorant and incapable men whom you put in command of your wars promptly become worthy enough, simply because you employ them" — which is very close to the custom of so many peoples who canonise the king they have chosen from their own ranks, and are not content to honour him but must adore him. The Mexicans, after the ceremonies of their king's coronation are over, dare no longer look him in the face but, as if they had deified him by his royalty. Among the oaths they make him take to uphold their religion, their laws, and their liberties, to be valiant, just, and mild, he further swears to make the sun run its course in its accustomed light, to drain the clouds in due season, to make rivers run their course, and to make the earth bear everything necessary for his people.

I differ from this common fashion, and am more apt to suspect a man's capacity when I see it accompanied by that grandeur of fortune and public applause. We have to consider what an advantage it is to be able to speak when one pleases, to choose one's subject, to interrupt or change it with magisterial authority, to fend off others' opposition by a nod, a smile, or silence, in front of an assembly that trembles with reverence and respect. A man of prodigious fortune, when called on to give his judgment on some slight dispute foolishly started up at his table, began with these words: "It can only be a liar or a fool who says otherwise than so-and-so." Pursue that philosophical point with a dagger in your hand.

There is another observation I have made, from which I draw great benefit: in conferences and disputes, not every word that seems good is to be accepted on the spot. Most men are rich in borrowed sufficiency: someone can say a good thing, give a good answer, cite a good sentence, without at all seeing the force of either the answer or the sentence. That a man may not understand all he borrows can perhaps be verified in myself. One must not always give in straight off, however much truth or beauty seems to lie in the opposing argument; either we must firmly meet it, or back off under cover of not understanding it, so as to test on every side how it sits in the author. It may happen that we entangle ourselves and help to reinforce the point itself. I have sometimes, in the heat of combat, made answers that hit home far beyond my expectation or hope; I gave them only as filler, they were received as full weight. As, when I contend with a vigorous man, I please myself by anticipating his conclusions, easing him of the trouble of explaining himself, trying to forestall his imagination while it is still springing and incomplete — the order and pertinence of his understanding warn and threaten me from afar — I deal in quite the opposite way with the others: I must understand nothing and presuppose nothing except by them. If they pronounce in general terms, "this is good, that is bad," and happen to be right, see whether it isn't fortune that has hit it for them; let them limit and circumscribe their judgment a little, say why, or how it is so. These universal judgments which I see everywhere are meaningless; they are like men who salute a whole crowd at once; those who really know take notice of individuals and greet them by name. But it's a risky undertaking; more than every day I have seen weak understandings, eager to look clever by picking out, as they read a book, what is best and most to be admired, fix their admiration on something so ill chosen that, instead of making us see the excellence of the author, they make us see their own ignorance perfectly well. The exclamation "That's fine" is safe enough, after having heard a whole page of Virgil; that's how the cunning sort save themselves. But to undertake to follow him line by line, with a trained and tested judgment, to observe where a good author surpasses himself, weighing the words, the phrases, the inventions, his various excellences one after another — stay clear of that:
"Videndum est, non modo quid quisque loquatur, sed etiam quid quisque sentiat, atque etiam qua de causa quisque sentiat."
["A man must examine not only what each person says, but also what each one thinks, and from what reason each one thinks it." — Cicero, De Offic., i. 41.]

Every day I hear fools say things that aren't foolish. They say a good thing; let's see how far they understand it, where they got it from, and what they mean by it. We help them make use of this fine expression, this fine sentence which isn't theirs; they only have it on loan; they've blurted it out at random; we set it up for them in credit and esteem. You're lending them a hand. To what end? They don't feel they owe you anything for it, and they grow even more inept. Don't help them; let them alone. They will handle the matter like people afraid of burning their fingers; they dare neither change its position nor light, nor break into it; jolt it ever so slightly, and it slips through their fingers; they let it go, however strong or beautiful it may be. They are fine weapons, but poorly hafted. How many times have I seen this proved? Now, if you go and explain something to them and try to confirm them in it, they snatch at it and immediately rob you of the credit of your interpretation: "That's just what I was about to say; that was exactly my idea; if I didn't express it that way, it was for lack of the right words." Hot air! Even malice must be brought into play to correct this arrogant ignorance. The doctrine of Hegesias, "that we are neither to hate nor accuse, but to instruct," is right elsewhere; but here it is injustice and inhumanity to help and set right a man who needs no help and is the worse for it. I love to let them sink deeper into the mire — so deep, if possible, that they may at last see their own error.

Folly and absurdity are not to be cured by mere admonition; what Cyrus answered to the man who urged him to harangue his army on the point of battle — "that men do not become valiant and warlike on the sudden, by a fine speech, any more than a man becomes a good musician by hearing a fine song" — may properly be said of an admonition like this. These are apprenticeships to be served beforehand, by long and continued training. We owe this care, this assiduity of correction and instruction, to our own people; but to go and preach to the first passer-by, to become tutor to the ignorance and folly of the first man we meet — that is a thing I detest. I rarely do it, even in private conversation, and would rather give the whole thing up than launch into these elementary, schoolmasterly lessons. My temper is unfit either to speak or write for beginners; but as for things said in common conversation, or in passing, I never oppose them by word or sign, however false or absurd.

As for the rest, nothing vexes me so much in folly as that it is more satisfied with itself than any sane reason can reasonably be. It is unfortunate that prudence forbids us to satisfy and trust ourselves, and always sends us away timorous and discontented, while obstinacy and rashness fill those possessed by them with joy and assurance. It is the most ignorant who look at other men over their shoulder, always coming back from the combat full of joy and triumph. And what's more, this arrogance of speech and gaiety of countenance usually gives them the upper hand in the audience's opinion, which is commonly weak and incapable of judging and discerning the real advantage. Obstinacy of opinion and heat in argument are the surest proofs of folly; is there anything so assured, resolute, disdainful, contemplative, serious, and grave as the donkey?

May we not include under the heading of conference and communication the quick and sharp repartees which mirth and familiarity introduce among friends, pleasantly and wittily jesting and rallying with one another? It's an exercise for which my natural cheerfulness makes me fit enough, and which, if not as tense and serious as the other I mentioned, is, as Lycurgus thought, no less keen and ingenious, and no less useful. For my part, I contribute more freedom than wit to it, and have more luck in it than invention; but I am perfect at taking it, for I endure a comeback that is not only tart but indiscreet too, without being at all moved; and when anyone attacks me, if I don't have a brisk answer ready straight away, I don't bother to pursue the point with a tedious and impertinent contest verging on obstinacy — I let it pass, drop my ears cheerfully, and put off my revenge to another and better time. There's no merchant who always wins. Most men change their countenance and voice when their wits fail them, and through ill-timed anger, instead of taking revenge, betray at once their folly and their impatience. In this kind of jollity, we sometimes pinch the secret strings of our imperfections which, at a graver moment, we could not touch without offence — and so we usefully give one another a hint of our defects. There are other kinds of horseplay, rude and indiscreet, in the French manner, which I hate mortally; my skin is very tender and sensitive. In my time I have seen two princes of the blood put in their graves on that very account. It is unhandsome to fight in play. For the rest, when I have a mind to judge anyone, I ask him how far he is content with himself, how much his speech or his work pleases him. I will have none of those fine excuses: "I only did it in sport,
'Ablatum mediis opus est incudibus istud.'
["That work was taken from the anvil half finished." — Ovid, Trist., i. 6, 29.]

I wasn't an hour at it; I haven't looked at it since." Well then, I say, set those aside and give me a finished one, the sort you'd have yourself measured by. And then, what do you think is the best thing in your work? Is it this part, or that? Is it the grace, the matter, the invention, the judgment, or the learning? For I find that men are usually as wide of the mark in judging their own work as they are in judging other people's — not only because of the affection they have for it, but for want of the capacity to know and distinguish it. The work, by its own force and fortune, may second the workman and sometimes outstrip him, beyond his invention and knowledge. For my part, I judge the value of other men's work more obscurely than that of my own; and I rate the Essays, now high, now low, with great doubt and inconstancy. There are several books that are useful because of their subjects, from which the author gets no praise; and good books, like good works, that shame their workman. I may write about the manner of our feasts and the fashion of our clothes, and write them ill; I may publish the edicts of my time and the letters of princes that pass from hand to hand; I may make an abridgment of a good book (and every abridgment of a good book is a foolish abridgment), which book then gets lost; and so on — posterity will get singular use out of such compositions, but what honour will I have from them, except by great good luck? Most famous books are of this kind.

When I read Philippe de Commines, doubtless a very good author, several years ago, I noticed this as no commonplace saying: "That a man must take care not to do his master so great a service that at last he won't know how to give him his just reward." But I ought to commend the invention, not him, because I came across it in Tacitus not long ago:
"Beneficia eo usque laeta sunt, dum videntur exsolvi posse; ubi multum antevenere, pro gratia odium redditur;"
["Benefits are welcome only as long as they seem capable of being repaid; when they go much beyond that, hatred is returned instead of thanks." — Tacitus, Annal., iv. 18.]
and Seneca puts it vigorously:
"Nam qui putat esse turpe non reddere, non vult esse cui reddat:"
["For he who thinks it shameful not to repay does not wish the man to be alive to whom he owes the return." — Seneca, Ep., 81.]
Q. Cicero puts it less pointedly:
"Qui se non putat satisfacere, amicus esse nullo modo potest."
["He who does not think he has done enough can in no way be a friend." — Q. Cicero, De Petitione Consulatus, c. 9.]

The subject, depending on what it is, may make an author look learned and of good memory; but to judge in him the parts that are most truly his own and most worthy — the vigour and beauty of his soul — one must first know what is his own and what is not; and in what is not his own, how much we owe him for the choice, arrangement, ornament, and language in which he has presented it. What if he has borrowed the matter and spoiled the form, as often happens? We, who are little read in books, find ourselves in this fix: when we meet a high-flying fancy in some new poet, or a strong argument in a preacher, we still don't dare to praise it until we have first asked some learned man whether it is the writer's own wit or borrowed from someone else; until then I always stay on my guard.

I have lately been reading right through the history of Tacitus, without interrupting it with anything else (which rarely happens with me — it being twenty years since I have stayed with any one book for an hour together), and I did it at the urging of a gentleman whom France much esteems, both for his own worth and on account of the constant form of capacity and virtue that runs through many of his brothers. I don't know any author who, in a public narrative, mixes in so much consideration of manners and individual inclinations; and I am of quite the opposite opinion to him, holding that, since he had especially to follow the lives of the emperors of his time, so various and extreme in every sort of form, and so many notable acts as their cruelty in particular produced in their subjects, he had a stronger and more attractive matter to handle than if he had had to describe battles and general upheavals. So I often find him sterile, hurrying over those brave deaths as if he feared to weary us with their number and length. This form of history is by far the most useful; public movements depend mostly on the conduct of fortune, private ones on our own. It is rather a judgment than a narration of history; there are more precepts in it than stories; it is not a book to read, it is a book to study and learn from; it is full of sententious opinions, right or wrong; it is a nursery of ethical and political discourses for the use and ornament of those who have any place in the government of the world. He always argues by strong and solid reasons, after a pointed and subtle manner, according to the affected style of that age, which was so in love with an inflated manner that, where point and subtlety were lacking in the matter, it supplied them with lofty and swelling words. The style is not unlike Seneca's: I find Tacitus more sinewy, and Seneca more sharp. His pen seems most suited to a troubled and sickly state, such as ours at present is; you would often say he paints and pinches us.

Those who doubt his good faith accuse themselves sufficiently of being his enemy on some other account. His opinions are sound, and lean to the right side in Roman affairs. And yet I am angry with him for judging Pompey more severely than is consistent with the opinion of those worthy men who lived in the same age and had dealings with him — and for having reckoned him on a par with Marius and Sylla, except that Pompey was more guarded. Other writers have not cleared his intentions in the management of affairs of ambition and revenge; even his friends were afraid that victory would have carried him beyond the bounds of reason — but not to so immeasurable a degree as theirs. Nothing in his life threatened such open cruelty and tyranny. Nor should we set suspicion against evidence; and so I do not believe Plutarch on this point. That Tacitus's narrations were genuine and straightforward may perhaps be argued from this very thing: that they do not always square with the conclusions of his judgments, which he follows according to the bias he has taken, often beyond the matter he presents — which he has not deigned to alter in the slightest. He needs no excuse for having approved the religion of his time, as the laws enjoined, and for having been ignorant of the true one; that was his misfortune, not his fault.

I have chiefly considered his judgment, and am not entirely satisfied with it throughout — as with these words in the letter that Tiberius, old and sick, sent to the senate: "What shall I write to you, sirs, or how should I write to you, or what should I not write to you at this time? May the gods and goddesses lay a worse punishment upon me than I am daily tormented with, if I know!" I don't see why he should so positively apply them to a sharp remorse tormenting Tiberius's conscience; at any rate, when I was in the same condition, I felt no such thing.

And this also seemed to me a little mean of him: that, having to say he had held an honourable office in Rome, he excuses himself by saying he doesn't mention it out of ostentation. That seems mean, I say, for such a soul as his; for not to speak frankly of oneself implies some want of courage. A man of solid and lofty judgment, who judges soundly and surely, makes use of his own example on every occasion, just as he does of other people's, and gives evidence about himself as freely as about a third party. We are to set aside these common rules of civility in favour of truth and freedom. I dare not only to speak of myself, but to speak only of myself; when I write of anything else, I lose my way and wander from my subject. I am not so indiscreetly in love with myself, so wholly mixed up with and bound to myself, that I cannot distinguish and consider myself apart, as I do a neighbour or a tree. It is equally a fault not to see how far one's worth extends, and to say more than a man finds in himself. We owe more love to God than to ourselves, and yet know him less, and speak of him as much as we please.

If the writings of Tacitus reveal anything true about his qualities, he was a great personage, upright and bold, of a virtue not superstitious but philosophical and generous. One may think him bold in his reporting — as where he tells us that a soldier carrying a load of wood had his hands so frozen and so stuck to the load that they stayed clenched and dead on it, severed from his arms. In such things I always defer to the authority of so great a witness.

What he also says — that Vespasian, by the favour of the god Serapis, cured a blind woman at Alexandria by anointing her eyes with his spittle, and I don't know what other miracle — he says following the example and duty of all his good historians. They record every event of importance; and among public happenings are the popular rumours and opinions. It is their part to relate common beliefs, not to regulate them; that part belongs to divines and philosophers, the directors of consciences. And so this fellow historian of his, and a great man like himself, very wisely said:
"Equidem plura transcribo, quam credo: nam nec affirmare sustineo, de quibus dubito, nec subducere quae accepi;"
["Truly, I set down more things than I believe, for I can neither affirm what I doubt, nor suppress what I have heard." — Quintus Curtius, ix.]
and this other:
"Haec neque affirmare neque refellere operae pretium est; famae rerum standum est."
["It is not worth the trouble to affirm or refute these things; we must stand by report." — Livy, i., Praef., and viii. 6.]

And writing in an age when belief in prodigies was beginning to decline, he says he would not, even so, leave off including them in his Annals and giving an account of things received by so many worthy men, and with such reverence of antiquity. Very well said. Let them deliver history to us more as they have received it than as they themselves believe it. I, who am sovereign over the matter I treat, and accountable to no one, do not, even so, always believe myself. I often hazard sallies of my own wit, in which I have much doubt of myself, and certain verbal quibbles at which I shake my own ears; but I let them go at a venture. I see that others get a reputation by such things: it is not for me alone to judge. I present myself standing and lying, before and behind, on my right and on my left, in all my natural postures. Wits, though equal in force, are not always equal in taste and application.
This is what my memory presents to me roughly, and with uncertainty enough; all judgments in the rough are weak and imperfect.
